# Sharp low-maximum centroid cap bounds in dimensions three and four

Let T_d=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), let u_i>=0 with sum_i u_i=1, and
assume max_i u_i<=2/(d+1). Let

    P_d(u)=|T_d intersect {u.x>=1/(d+1)}|/|T_d|.

Then

    P_3(u)>=1/2,
    P_4(u)>=13/27.                                     (1)

Both constants are attained. In dimension four the lower value is
attained at u=(2/5,2/5,1/10,1/10), up to permutation. In particular,

    P_d(u)>=(7/6)(d/(d+1))^d       for d=3,4.           (2)

This is a finite-dimensional ordinary cap theorem. It does not assert
a bound for all dimensions or a mixed-integer center theorem.

## 1. Exact exponential coordinates

Let E_0,...,E_d be independent standard exponential variables. Uniform
barycentric coordinates of a simplex are E_i/sum_j E_j, as follows
directly by the total-mass/barycentric change of variables in their
joint density. Put

    a_0=-1,       a_i=(d+1)u_i-1 for i>=1.

Then -1<=a_i<=1, sum_i a_i=0, and

    P_d(u)=P(sum_i a_i E_i>=0).                         (3)

Terms with coefficient zero may be discarded. The independent sums
with positive coefficients have continuous densities, so equality at
the threshold has probability zero. We will use elementary exponential
Laplace transforms and handle coincident coefficients by continuity.
Such continuity follows, for example, by using the same exponential
variables while varying the coefficients: the indicators converge
almost surely off the null equality event, and bounded convergence
applies.

If all d remaining coefficients are nonnegative, their sum is one.
Conditioning on them against E_0 gives

    P_d(u)=1-product_(i=1)^d(1+a_i)^(-1)>=1/2,           (4)

because product_i(1+a_i)>=1+sum_i a_i=2. If there is only one
positive coefficient, it must equal one, since all positive
coefficients are <=1 and the fixed negative coefficient is -1.
Every other coefficient is then zero, and the probability is 1/2.

## 2. Two positive and two negative coefficients

Suppose the nonzero coefficient list is p,q,-1,-c, where

    0<p,q<=1,       0<=c<=1,       p+q=1+c.

For p!=q the survival function of pE_1+qE_2 is

    [p exp(-x/p)-q exp(-x/q)]/(p-q),       x>=0.

Integrating against E_0+cE_3 and simplifying gives

    P(pE_1+qE_2>=E_0+cE_3)-1/2
      =[(pq-c)(pq+c)]
         /[2(p+1)(q+1)(p+c)(q+c)].                     (5)

For a direct check of the simplification, let S=p+q=1+c and P=pq.
The numerator of the probability over the displayed denominator
without its factor two is

    N=P^2+(S^2-c)P+cS^2,

and twice N minus that denominator is P^2-c^2. The case p=q follows
by the continuity just justified. All denominators in (5) are positive.

Finally

    pq-c=(1-p)(1-q)>=0,

so (5) is nonnegative. This proves the d=3 assertion: after discarding
zero coefficients, the only case not covered by (4) or the single
positive case has precisely this sign pattern. The value 1/2 is
attained, for example, by u=(1/2,1/4,1/4).

## 3. Three positive and two negative coefficients

For dimension four, next suppose the coefficients are p,q,r,-1,-c,
with p,q,r in (0,1], 0<=c<=1, and p+q+r=1+c. Put

    e_2=pq+pr+qr,       e_3=pqr,
    A=(1+p)(1+q)(1+r)=2+c+e_2+e_3,
    B=(c+p)(c+q)(c+r)=c^2+2c^3+c e_2+e_3.

Integrating the survival function of E_0+cE_4 against the positive
sum gives, initially for c!=1,

    probability=1-[A^(-1)-c^4 B^(-1)]/(1-c).

Clearing denominators and cancelling 1-c yields the exact identity

    probability-1/2
      =[e_3^2+(1+c)(e_2-c)e_3+c(e_2-c)(e_2+c)]/(2AB). (6)

It also holds at c=1 by continuity. Positivity of p,q,r makes A,B
positive, including c=0. Since p,q,r<=1,

    (1-p)(1-q)(1-r)=e_2-e_3-c>=0,

so e_2-c>=e_3>=0. Every term in the numerator of (6) is nonnegative.
Thus this entire sign pattern has probability at least 1/2.

## 4. Two positive and three negative coefficients

The only remaining potentially smaller case in dimension four has
coefficients p,q,-1,-c,-e, where p,q in (0,1], c,e>=0, and
p+q=1+c+e. Write

    C=c+e,       Q=ce,       P=pq,       S=1+C=p+q.

The coefficient restrictions imply

    0<=C<=1,
    0<=Q<=C^2/4,
    P>=C,

where the last inequality follows from P-C=(1-p)(1-q)>=0.

Integrating the same two-exponential positive survival function now
against E_0+cE_3+eE_4 gives the probability N/D, with

    N=P^3+[S^2-(C+Q)]P^2
        +[(C+Q)S^2-2QS]P+QS^3,

    D=(P+C+2)[P^2+(C+2C^2-2Q)P+QS(S+C)+Q^2].          (7)

These identities extend from p!=q to p=q by continuity. The denominator
is positive: it is exactly

    (p+1)(q+1)(p+c)(q+c)(p+e)(q+e).

We prove 27N-13D>=0. At fixed C and P this is a concave quadratic
in Q, with leading coefficient -13(P+C+2)<0. Its minimum on
[0,C^2/4] therefore occurs at an endpoint. At Q=0, one of c,e is
zero, so Section 2 applies and the probability is at least 1/2,
which is larger than 13/27.

At the other endpoint Q=C^2/4, put X=P-C>=0. Direct polynomial
expansion gives

    27N-13D
      =14X^3+(1+43C+3C^2/4)X^2
        +(3C+36C^2-3C^3/4-9C^4/16)X
        +(9/8)C^2(1-C)(C^2+6C+2).                     (8)

All terms are nonnegative for 0<=C<=1 and X>=0. For the only
coefficient with negative displayed terms, use

    3C+36C^2-3C^3/4-9C^4/16
       >=3C+(555/16)C^2>=0.

Thus (8) is nonnegative, and concavity in Q proves the desired
inequality throughout its permitted interval. This establishes
probability>=13/27 in the last sign pattern.

At C=1, P=1, Q=1/4, equality holds in (8). These parameters give
p=q=1 and c=e=1/2, hence the normal
u=(2/5,2/5,1/10,1/10). Its exact cap fraction is 13/27. For an
independent geometric integration, see
`candidate f670e4af83fa9465`.

## 5. Exhaustion of cases and the weaker sufficient constants

In dimension four, four nonnegative remaining coefficients are covered
by (4), three positives by Section 3, two positives by Section 4,
and one positive by the symmetric exponential case. Zero coefficients
are included by dropping them or by continuity. Hence no sign pattern
or boundary case is omitted. This proves (1) completely.

The exact margins above the proposed sufficient constants are

    1/2-(7/6)(3/4)^3=1/128>0,
    13/27-(7/6)(4/5)^4=61/16875>0.

This proves (2) in these two dimensions, without an unproved
coefficient concentration principle or a generic mean/support
relaxation. The corresponding all-dimensional inequality remains
unproved here.
